hero.text: There is more than one IELTS test, and preparing for the wrong one is the costliest mistake a candidate can make. Find the one your university, employer or visa asks for, then practise that test.

blocks.title: Check the official requirements
text: RCF English is not connected with IELTS, the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment. Test formats, fees, dates and the tests accepted for a particular purpose can change. **Before you book, confirm which test you need with the organisation that asked for it, and check the details on [ielts.org](https://ielts.org).**

blocks.heading: The IELTS tests at a glance
rows: **IELTS Academic**
University study at undergraduate or postgraduate level, and professional registration (for example, some medical and nursing bodies)
Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking. Reading and Writing use academic-style material.
**IELTS General Training**
Work, training, secondary education and migration to some English-speaking countries
Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking. Reading and Writing use everyday and workplace material.
**IELTS for UKVI** (Academic or General Training)
Some UK visa and immigration applications that require a Secure English Language Test
The same content and format as Academic or General Training, taken at an approved UKVI test centre.
**IELTS Life Skills** (A1, A2, B1)
Some UK visa applications, such as certain family, settlement and citizenship routes
Speaking and Listening only, at one level, with a pass or fail result.

blocks.heading: Academic and General Training: what is the same and what is different
blocks.caption: The two tests share Listening and Speaking. The difference is in Reading and Writing.
rows: Listening
30 minutes, 4 parts, 40 questions. **The same for both.**
The same as Academic
Reading
60 minutes, 3 long passages from books, journals and magazines, 40 questions
60 minutes, 40 questions in 3 sections: everyday texts such as notices and advertisements, workplace texts, and one longer general-interest passage
Writing Task 1
Describe a graph, table, chart, map or process in at least 150 words
Write a letter (formal, semi-formal or personal) in at least 150 words
Writing Task 2
An essay in at least 250 words on an academic-style topic
An essay in at least 250 words on a topic of general interest
Speaking
11 to 14 minutes, face to face with an examiner, 3 parts. **The same for both.**
The same as Academic

blocks.heading: IELTS for UKVI
text: IELTS for UKVI is not a different kind of English test. It is the **Academic or General Training test with the same questions, format and marking**, taken at a test centre approved by UK Visas and Immigration, under extra identity and security checks, so that the result can be used for certain UK visa applications.

Prepare for it exactly as you would for Academic or General Training. What matters is booking the **UKVI** version when your visa route asks for a Secure English Language Test; an ordinary IELTS result may not be accepted for that purpose.

blocks.heading: IELTS Life Skills
text: IELTS Life Skills tests **only Speaking and Listening**, at one level of the Common European Framework: **A1**, **A2** or **B1**. It is taken with one examiner and one other candidate, and the result is simply **pass** or **fail**.

It is used for some UK visa routes where the Home Office asks for a particular level. The tasks are about everyday life: talking about yourself, your family and your routine, making arrangements, and understanding short spoken information.

Practise speaking in full sentences about familiar topics, asking the other candidate questions, and listening for specific details such as times, places and prices. The [IELTS Speaking](practical-english/ielts/speaking/) and [IELTS Listening](practical-english/ielts/listening/) pages on this site will help, as will [Everyday English](general-english/everyday-english/).

blocks.heading: Paper, computer and One Skill Retake
text: **Paper-based and computer-delivered.** Academic and General Training can be taken on paper or on a computer at a test centre. The questions and the marking are the same. On computer, Listening gives a short time to check answers instead of ten minutes to transfer them to an answer sheet. **The Speaking test is always a live conversation with an examiner.**
**IELTS Online.** In some places an online version can be taken at home under remote supervision. Check whether the organisation you are applying to accepts it before choosing it.

**One Skill Retake.** In some locations, candidates who took the computer-delivered test can retake one of the four skills, within a set period, instead of the whole test. Availability depends on the country and test centre, and not every organisation accepts a retaken result, so check both before relying on it.

blocks.title: Instructions
text: You have **60 minutes** for all three sections and all 40 questions. Write your answers as you go: there is no transfer time.
Sections 1 and 2 are shorter and easier. Aim to finish them in about 35 minutes so that you have 25 minutes for Section 3.

blocks.heading: Section 1
text: *Questions 1 to 14*

parts.heading: Parkside Leisure Centre: Swimming Pool Information
text: **Opening hours.** The pool is open from 6.30 a.m. to 9.30 p.m. Monday to Friday, and from 8.00 a.m. to 6.00 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. On the first Monday of every month the pool is closed until 2.00 p.m. for deep cleaning.
**Lane swimming.** Between 6.30 a.m. and 9.00 a.m. on weekdays the pool is divided into slow, medium and fast lanes. Please choose the lane that matches your speed and swim in a clockwise direction.
**Family sessions.** Family sessions run from 10.00 a.m. to 1.00 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. Inflatable toys are brought out on Sundays only.
**Children.** Children under eight must be accompanied in the water by an adult aged sixteen or over. One adult may supervise a maximum of two children under eight.
**What to wear.** Swimming caps are not compulsory, but long hair must be tied back. Please shower before entering the pool.
**Lockers.** Lockers take a returnable coin, which you get back when you open the locker again. The centre is not responsible for valuables left in changing areas.
**Lessons.** Classes for adult beginners are held on Tuesday and Thursday evenings. Places are limited and must be booked at reception at least one week in advance.

parts.heading: Questions 1-7

The pool is cleaned on the first Monday of every month.

An adult may take three children under eight into the pool.
Swimming caps can be bought at reception.
Adult beginners' lessons must be booked in advance.

parts.heading: Westbrook Adult Education College: Evening Courses
text: **A   Digital Photography.** Eight weeks, Monday evenings. Learn to compose better pictures and edit them. No experience is needed, and a phone camera is perfectly acceptable.

**B   Conversational Spanish.** Ten weeks, Wednesday evenings. For learners who already know some basic Spanish and want to speak with more confidence. This course is not suitable for complete beginners.

**C   Home Electrical Safety.** A single full-day workshop on a Saturday. Find out how to check wiring, replace plugs and fuses safely, and when to call a professional. Everyone who completes the workshop receives a certificate.
**D   Creative Writing.** Six weeks. All sessions take place online by video call, so you can join from home. Participants share a short piece of writing each week.
**E   Bread and Pastry Baking.** Five weeks, Thursday evenings. All ingredients are included in the course fee, and aprons are provided.

blocks.heading: Section 2
text: *Questions 15 to 27*

parts.heading: Harbourline Logistics: A Guide for New Warehouse Staff
text: **Your first day.** Please report to the security gate at 7.45 a.m. on your first day. Bring photographic identification and the completed form with your bank details, so that you can be added to the payroll. You will be given a high-visibility vest at the gate, which must be worn at all times on site.

**Induction.** The first two days are an induction programme covering health and safety, fire procedures and the warehouse layout. For your own safety, you may not operate any equipment, including pallet trucks, until you have completed the induction.

**Safety footwear.** Steel-toe boots must be worn in the warehouse at all times. The company provides every new member of staff with one pair free of charge. If your boots are damaged or wear out, replacement pairs are available from the stores office at half the normal price.
**Breaks and meals.** A full shift includes a thirty-minute lunch break and two fifteen-minute rest breaks. Hot meals are available in the staff canteen at a subsidised price.
**Parking.** Staff should use the car park at the rear of the building. Motorcycles and bicycles must be left in the covered bay beside the canteen, not in the car park.
**Changing shifts.** If you wish to swap a shift with a colleague, both of you must obtain the approval of your team leader at least 48 hours before the shift.

parts.heading: Annual Leave: How to Request Time Off
text: **Entitlement.** Full-time staff are entitled to 21 days of paid annual leave each year, in addition to public holidays. After five years of continuous service, this rises to 25 days.

**Making a request.** All requests must be made through the online staff portal. Requests for more than five working days must be made at least four weeks in advance; requests for shorter periods need two weeks' notice.

**December.** Because December is the busiest month, no more than two members of any team may be on leave at the same time. Where more people ask for the same dates, leave is given in order of the date on which the requests were made.
**Unused leave.** Up to five days of unused leave may be carried over into the following year, but these days must be taken before the end of March.

**Illness during leave.** If you are ill while on annual leave, send a medical certificate to the human resources office within seven days of returning to work, and the days of illness will be returned to your leave balance.

parts.heading: Questions 22-27

Where must staff make their leave requests?

In December, what decides who gets leave when too many people ask for the same dates?

blocks.heading: Section 3
text: *Questions 28 to 40*

parts.heading: Mending the Throwaway Habit
text: **A**   It is ten o'clock on a Saturday morning, and a community hall is filling up. Along one wall, volunteers sit behind tables covered in screwdrivers, soldering irons, sewing machines and reels of thread. Opposite them, a queue has formed: a man with a table lamp that flickers, a woman carrying a jacket with a broken zip, a teenager holding a laptop that will not charge. Nobody is paying, and nobody is selling anything. This is a repair café, and the only rule on the poster by the door is that you must stay with the thing you have brought.

**B**   The idea began in Amsterdam in 2009, when a single event was organised to see whether neighbours would bring broken belongings to be mended by other neighbours. They did, in numbers that surprised the organisers, and the model was simple enough to copy. Within a few years similar events were running in towns across Europe, and by the early 2020s there were more than two thousand repair cafés around the world, most of them meeting once a month in libraries, church halls and community centres.

**C**   Behind their popularity lies a frustration that many people share. A generation ago, a broken radio or kettle was taken to a repair shop as a matter of course. Today, many products are designed in ways that make repair difficult: cases are glued together rather than held with screws, and the replacement parts that would allow a simple fix are often impossible to buy. Even when repair is technically possible, the cost of an hour's skilled labour can be greater than the price of a new item, so buying a replacement is frequently cheaper. The result is that objects which could work for years more are thrown away.

**D**   The rule that owners stay beside their item is not a matter of convenience for the volunteers. Organisers explain that watching, and often helping, is the real purpose of the visit. A person who has seen a volunteer open a toaster, find a loose connection and fix it is far less likely to see such objects as mysterious, and far more likely to attempt a similar repair at home next time. Many visitors say that the confidence they take away is worth more to them than the repair itself.

**E**   The cafés have also become meeting places. For people who live alone, a morning spent talking to a volunteer over a broken clock can be a rare opportunity for conversation. Many volunteers are retired, and the skills they spent a working life acquiring, from tailoring to electronics, are once again valued by others. It is common to see a volunteer in his seventies explaining a circuit to a student, while at the next table a young visitor shows an older one how to back up the photographs on a phone.

**F**   Not everyone is convinced that the movement can achieve very much. Volunteers themselves admit that some items cannot be saved, and some cafés refuse to work on appliances connected to the mains because of safety concerns. Critics point out that the number of objects mended each month is tiny compared with the quantity of electrical waste a country produces, and argue that the responsibility for designing products that last should lie with manufacturers rather than with unpaid volunteers.

**G**   There are signs that governments have been listening. In several places, including the European Union, rules introduced in recent years require the makers of certain household appliances to keep spare parts available for a number of years after a model is sold, and to make repair information available to professional repairers. Campaigners describe these laws as a first step rather than a solution, but they note that the question of whether a product can be mended is now being discussed in parliaments as well as in community halls.

text: Both tasks were written by RCF English. This is not an official IELTS test.

blocks.heading: Writing Task 1
text: *You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.*
You recently stayed at a hotel while attending a two-day work conference. After you returned home, you realised that you had left something in your room.
**Write a letter to the manager of the hotel. In your letter:**
bullets: give the dates of your stay and explain why you were there
describe the item you left behind
say what you would like the hotel to do

text: *Write at least 150 words. You do* **NOT** *need to write any addresses. Begin your letter as follows:* **Dear Sir or Madam,**

blocks.heading: What Task 1 is marked on
columns: What the examiner looks for in a letter
rows: Task Achievement
All three bullet points covered and developed, the purpose clear from the start, and a tone that suits writing to a manager you have never met: polite and formal.
Coherence and Cohesion
One paragraph for each bullet point, in a logical order, joined with natural linking words.
Lexical Resource
Precise words for the item and the situation, used accurately and without repetition.
Grammatical Range and Accuracy
A mix of simple and complex sentences, with polite request forms such as *I would be grateful if you could...*

blocks.heading: Writing Task 2
text: *You should spend about 40 minutes on this task. Write about the following topic:*
**In many countries, young people are encouraged to do unpaid voluntary work in their local community. Some people believe that this should be compulsory for all secondary school students.**
**To what extent do you agree or disagree?**
*Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.heading: What Task 2 is marked on
columns: What the examiner looks for in the essay
rows: Task Response

A clear position on *compulsory* voluntary work, held throughout, with main ideas that are developed and supported. An essay about volunteering in general, which never deals with *compulsory*, is off the point.
Coherence and Cohesion
An introduction that states the position, body paragraphs with one central idea each, and a conclusion that follows from them.
Lexical Resource
Topic vocabulary used precisely: *civic responsibility, work experience, obligation, genuine commitment*.
Grammatical Range and Accuracy
Accurate complex sentences, including conditionals and concessions such as *Although...*

blocks.title: End of the Writing test
text: Compare your answers with the [model letter and model essay](practical-english/ielts/general-training-test-1/answers/#writing). For more essays, see the [10 Task 2 model essays](practical-english/ielts/model-essays/). Then sit [Practice Test 1: Speaking](practical-english/ielts/practice-test-1/speaking/), which is the same for both tests.

blocks.heading: Model letter: Task 1
text: Dear Sir or Madam,

I stayed at your hotel from 12 to 14 March while attending the regional sales conference held in your conference suite, and I am writing because I believe I left a personal item in my room, number 318.

The item is a small black leather wallet containing my work identity card, two bank cards and a family photograph. I think I left it in the drawer of the bedside table on the morning I checked out, as I remember putting it there before I went to breakfast. Although the bank cards have now been cancelled, the photograph is of great sentimental value to me and cannot be replaced.

I would be very grateful if you could ask your housekeeping staff to check the room and your lost property records. If the wallet is found, could you please send it to me by registered post? I will, of course, pay any postage costs. Alternatively, I could arrange for a colleague who lives nearby to collect it.
Thank you in advance for your help. I look forward to hearing from you.
Yours faithfully,
Nadeesha Perera

parts.heading: Why this letter works
bullets: **The purpose is clear in the first sentence**, together with the dates and the reason for the stay: bullet point one is done immediately.
**The description is specific** (colour, material, contents, where it was left), and the photograph gives a reason why the matter still matters after the cards were cancelled.
**The request is polite and practical**, with an alternative, which develops bullet point three beyond a single sentence.
**Register is consistent:** *Dear Sir or Madam* is closed with *Yours faithfully*. About 180 words: comfortably over 150 without padding.

blocks.heading: Model essay: Task 2
text: Voluntary work in the community is widely praised, and it is tempting to conclude that something so beneficial should be required of every secondary school student. While I agree that schools should actively encourage volunteering, I believe that making it compulsory would undermine the very qualities that make it valuable.

Those in favour of compulsion make a strong case. Unpaid work can teach young people responsibility, introduce them to people from different backgrounds and give them practical experience that no classroom can provide. A requirement would also ensure that these benefits reach every student, not only those whose families already value community service. In countries where volunteering is part of the school curriculum, many students discover an interest they would never have found on their own.

However, the defining feature of voluntary work is that it is freely chosen. When it becomes an obligation, many students will treat it as one more box to tick, completing the minimum number of hours with little genuine commitment. Community organisations, which depend on reliable and willing helpers, may find themselves supervising reluctant teenagers rather than receiving real assistance. Furthermore, a compulsory scheme would fall hardest on students who already work part-time to support their families, adding to the pressure on those with the least free time.

A better approach, in my view, is for schools to make volunteering easy and attractive: arranging placements, recognising participation on school reports and allowing students to choose causes that matter to them. This keeps the benefits while preserving the element of choice.
In conclusion, although community service has clear value for young people, I disagree that it should be compulsory, because obligation tends to replace genuine commitment with reluctant compliance.

parts.heading: Why this essay works
bullets: **The position is stated in the introduction and never changes:** encourage, but do not make compulsory.
**The opposing view is given properly** before being answered, which shows balance without sitting on the fence.
**Every body paragraph has one central idea**, supported with a reason and a consequence rather than a list.
**The fourth paragraph offers an alternative**, which strengthens the argument instead of simply rejecting the proposal. About 300 words.
